grading: one point per correct answer; one answer per question

questions.question: A FortiGate advertises community 65000:200 even though the primary ISP SLA is healthy. Both BGP sessions are Established. Which check best isolates the preferred-map selection?

choices.text: Clear the local routing table and relearn connected routes.
choices.feedback: The issue is outbound advertisement policy, not local connected-route installation.

choices.text: Increase the BGP hold timer on the primary neighbor.
choices.feedback: Timers affect session liveness, not which outbound route map is selected.

choices.text: Compare the BGP neighbor's SD-WAN role, member, health-check and SLA-ID binding.
choices.feedback: The preferred map is selected from peer preference state; a healthy probe alone does not prove that binding exists.

choices.text: Change the remote ISP's local preference for received routes.
choices.feedback: That changes the remote AS's path selection, not the FortiGate's map choice.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the two outbound route-map fields?

choices.text: The normal map stays active while the preferred map changes local forwarding.
choices.feedback: Outbound maps filter advertisements; they do not select the FortiGate's local WAN path.

choices.text: The normal map is fallback; the preferred map applies when SD-WAN marks the peer preferred.
choices.feedback: This is the documented selection rule for the two outbound BGP map fields.

choices.text: The preferred map is for IPv6 only; the normal map is for IPv4 only.
choices.feedback: IPv4 and IPv6 each have normal and preferred outbound map fields.

choices.text: The preferred map filters inbound routes; the normal map handles redistribution policy.
choices.feedback: Inbound filtering and redistribution use different route-map attachment points.

questions.question: A preferred route map works for IPv4 but the IPv6 peer still advertises the fallback community. What should be checked?

choices.text: The ISP's MTU should be increased to 9000 bytes.
choices.feedback: MTU does not determine which BGP outbound route map is applied.

choices.text: The FortiGate DNS database and FQDN cache.
choices.feedback: DNS resolution does not select the IPv6 outbound BGP route map.

choices.text: The IPv4 route-map rule IDs should be renumbered.
choices.feedback: IPv4 rule order does not repair an unconfigured IPv6 neighbor field.

choices.text: The IPv6 neighbor's route-map-out6-preferable and IPv6 match objects.
choices.feedback: IPv6 has separate preferred and normal outbound map fields and address-family match objects.

questions.question: A BGP neighbor is Established and pingable, but the preferred advertisement is not selected. What does that evidence fail to prove?

choices.text: That the peer is preferred in the SD-WAN neighbor/health-check state.
choices.feedback: Reachability and BGP adjacency do not prove the SD-WAN preferred role is active.

choices.text: That the peer's TCP port is reachable.
choices.feedback: An Established session already demonstrates a working BGP transport.

choices.text: That the local route exists in the RIB.
choices.feedback: A BGP session does not by itself prove every candidate route is installed.

choices.text: That the route map has a name.
choices.feedback: A configured name does not prove match behavior, but the key missing evidence is preferred state.

questions.question: A global package is assigned to an ADOM, but header rules do not appear after the package was cloned and renamed. What is the safest first repair?

choices.text: Delete the local ADOM and recreate all managed devices.
choices.feedback: That is unnecessarily destructive and does not target the suspected metadata.

choices.text: Back up FortiManager, run the targeted invalid-global-assignment CDB check, then reassign.
choices.feedback: The documented procedure targets stale global assignment metadata and begins with a backup.

choices.text: Install the unchanged package repeatedly until the header appears.
choices.feedback: Installation cannot repair stale assignment metadata in the configuration database.

choices.text: Import the global header rules back from the FortiGate.
choices.feedback: Global header/footer policies are not imported back from managed device configuration.

questions.question: What does a successful Global Policy Package assignment prove?

choices.text: The ADOM version is irrelevant because global packages ignore version compatibility.
choices.feedback: FortiManager restricts assignment to compatible ADOM versions.

choices.text: Every managed FortiGate has already received the new header and footer rules.
choices.feedback: Assignment synchronizes the ADOM model; a device install is still required.

choices.text: Global objects were copied back automatically from each managed FortiGate device.
choices.feedback: Global Database objects are not reconstructed from managed device configuration.

choices.text: The package is synchronized into the ADOM, but device installation remains separate.
choices.feedback: Assignment and installation are distinct operations.

questions.question: A team wants a global package on every local policy package except two. Which assignment scope matches that requirement?

choices.text: Specify Policy Packages to Exclude.
choices.feedback: The exclusion option applies the global package to all packages except the listed ones.

choices.text: Specify Policy Packages to Include.
choices.feedback: The inclusion option applies only to listed packages.

choices.text: Assign only used objects.
choices.feedback: That setting controls object scope, not which packages receive the global package.

choices.text: Leave metadata variables unresolved.
choices.feedback: That controls variable resolution, not assignment scope.

questions.question: After unassigning a global policy package, why is a device installation still required?

choices.text: Downgrade the ADOM version before removing the assigned global package.
choices.feedback: Version downgrade is not the device-side removal mechanism.

choices.text: The Global Database deletes the package only after a managed-device reboot.
choices.feedback: A reboot is not the documented removal workflow.

choices.text: The device must receive an install that removes previously installed global rules.
choices.feedback: Unassignment changes the FortiManager model; install removes the device policy.

choices.text: The FortiGate must re-import its configuration into Global Database first.
choices.feedback: Global header/footer policies cannot be retrieved from the managed device.

questions.question: An analyst selects two values in the Explorer Source quick filter and receives zero results. What is the most likely interpretation?

choices.text: The timeline view hides related alerts whenever multiple filters are selected.
choices.feedback: Timeline visibility is separate from the quick-filter result set.

choices.text: The filter uses OR, and the empty result proves that log ingestion stopped.
choices.feedback: Multiple quick-filter values are combined with AND.

choices.text: The alert handler was disabled automatically when the filter was selected.
choices.feedback: Selecting a filter does not disable the handler.

choices.text: The quick filters combine with AND, further narrowing the alert result set.
choices.feedback: Multiple selected values narrow the result set using AND semantics.

questions.question: The Explorer timeline is blank immediately after an 8.0 upgrade, while related alerts are visible. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Rebuild the FortiAnalyzer database to restore the missing timeline chart.
choices.feedback: The documented default is a disabled timeline view, not a database fault.

choices.text: Enable the timeline in View Options; FortiAnalyzer 8.0 disables it by default.
choices.feedback: The 8.0 Explorer timeline is disabled by default.

choices.text: Reinstall FortiGate log-forwarding policies to repopulate the timeline chart.
choices.feedback: Visible related alerts show that the Explorer already has alert records.

choices.text: Change the alert-handler group-by fields to add a timeline dimension.
choices.feedback: Group-by fields affect Source/Target meaning, not timeline visibility.

questions.question: An alert's Source field shows a username and Target shows a server. What determines those labels?

choices.text: The order in which the triggering log records arrived at FortiAnalyzer.
choices.feedback: Arrival order does not define the alert's Source and Target labels.

choices.text: The physical ingress and egress interfaces on the source FortiGate.
choices.feedback: Those fields may represent identities or assets rather than packet interfaces.

choices.text: The alert handler's configured group-by fields define Source and Target labels.
choices.feedback: The handler determines which attributes populate those fields.

choices.text: The endpoint's current default gateway and routing table entries.
choices.feedback: Routing state does not define the alert handler's group-by fields.

questions.question: Which evidence best connects an alert row to the rule that generated it?

choices.text: Open Details and inspect the alert handler, rule, and Triggering Logs.
choices.feedback: The Details pane exposes the alert, handler, logs and rules.

choices.text: Check only the severity color in the related-alert table.
choices.feedback: Severity is a triage attribute, not rule provenance.

choices.text: Inspect only the FortiGate interface counters.
choices.feedback: Interface counters do not identify the FortiAnalyzer handler rule.

choices.text: Export the dashboard without opening the alert.
choices.feedback: A dashboard export may summarize counts but not expose the triggering rule chain.

questions.question: A FortiSwitch VXLAN interface is configured, but no tunnel is created. Which underlay condition is explicitly required?

choices.text: The outgoing interface must use DHCP to renew the VTEP address.
choices.feedback: DHCP mode is explicitly documented as unreliable for VXLAN.

choices.text: The tunnel IP must be a configured static primary address on the outgoing interface.
choices.feedback: The guide requires a static primary IP; a DHCP-mode interface is unreliable.

choices.text: The VNI must equal the remote switch's management VLAN.
choices.feedback: VNI and local VLAN are separate identifiers.

choices.text: The underlay must run IGMP snooping on every routed hop.
choices.feedback: IGMP snooping is not supported in the VXLAN underlay.

questions.question: Which configuration field maps the local VLAN to the overlay segment identifier?

choices.text: ip-version selects the VLAN tag and VNI.
choices.feedback: ip-version selects IPv4 multicast or unicast transport.

choices.text: remote-ip maps the local VLAN to the VNI.
choices.feedback: remote-ip identifies a VTEP address, not a VLAN mapping.

choices.text: interface sets the VNI and remote VLAN.
choices.feedback: interface selects the outgoing underlay interface.

choices.text: vlanid maps the local VLAN while vni identifies the VXLAN segment.
choices.feedback: The two values belong to different namespaces and are configured separately.

questions.question: The VXLAN interface exists, but remote MAC entries never appear. Which diagnostic pair is most useful?

choices.text: Clear all VLANs and reboot the switch.
choices.feedback: This is destructive and does not isolate the VXLAN learning path.

choices.text: Check only the switch serial number and PoE budget.
choices.feedback: Those values do not show VTEP reachability or remote MAC learning.

choices.text: Check the underlay route and use diagnose switch vxlan mac-address list.
choices.feedback: The route proves VTEP reachability; the MAC list shows whether remote addresses were learned.

choices.text: Check only the local access-port link state.
choices.feedback: A local link does not prove remote VTEP reachability.

questions.question: Which statement about IGMP snooping is correct for FortiSwitch VXLAN?

choices.text: Underlay snooping is unsupported; eligible access VLANs can use IGMP snooping.
choices.feedback: FortiSwitch distinguishes the unsupported underlay from model-dependent access-VLAN support.

choices.text: Enable IGMP snooping on every underlay router to support VXLAN flooding.
choices.feedback: IGMP snooping is not supported in the VXLAN underlay network.

choices.text: Unicast VXLAN tunnels require IGMP snooping to learn remote MAC addresses.
choices.feedback: Remote MAC learning and unicast VXLAN do not require underlay IGMP snooping.

choices.text: IGMP snooping replaces the local VNI-to-VLAN mapping on each switch.
choices.feedback: VNI and VLAN mapping remains an explicit VXLAN interface setting.

questions.question: A G-series AP does not offer channels 169, 173, or 177. What prerequisite should be checked first?

choices.text: Change the FortiGate system DNS server to refresh the AP channel list.
choices.feedback: DNS does not control the regulatory channel set.

choices.text: Increase 2.4 GHz transmit power before enabling additional 5 GHz channels.
choices.feedback: Transmit power does not enable UNII-4 channel availability.

choices.text: Enable WPA3 Enterprise on the SSID before selecting UNII-4 channels.
choices.feedback: SSID authentication does not determine the AP radio channel list.

choices.text: Confirm Single 5G mode and a country code that permits UNII-4.
choices.feedback: UNII-4 requires the supported platform mode and a permissive regulatory domain.

questions.question: Dedicated Scan is disabled on a supported Single-5G profile. What additional setting exposes UNII-4?

choices.text: Enable Dynamic VLAN assignment on the SSID before editing radio channels.
choices.feedback: Dynamic VLAN does not expose the radio's UNII-4 channel group.

choices.text: Enable the UNII-4 5GHz band option in the FortiAP profile.
choices.feedback: With Dedicated Scan disabled, the profile exposes this explicit control.

choices.text: Set the AP to Dual 5G mode to expose the additional UNII-4 channels.
choices.feedback: Dual 5G mode makes UNII-4 unavailable.

choices.text: Enable 802.11r fast roaming to unlock the UNII-4 channel list.
choices.feedback: Fast roaming does not control the radio's regulatory channel set.

questions.question: What is the documented radio-resource trade-off when UNII-4 is enabled?

choices.text: UNII-5 and UNII-6 channels become unavailable on Radio 3.
choices.feedback: The guide explicitly warns that enabling UNII-4 resets Radio 3's UNII-5/6 channel lists.

choices.text: Radio 2 loses all channels below 149.
choices.feedback: Radio 2 gains UNII-4 channels; lower channels are not removed by this setting.

choices.text: The AP disables its Ethernet uplink.
choices.feedback: The change affects radio channel allocation, not the wired uplink.

choices.text: The AP switches automatically to Dual 5G mode.
choices.feedback: UNII-4 is only available in Single 5G mode.

questions.question: The profile shows UNII-4 enabled. What does that not prove?

choices.text: That Radio 3 will retain its UNII-5 and UNII-6 channel options.
choices.feedback: Enabling UNII-4 removes those channel groups from Radio 3.

choices.text: That the controller profile contains the UNII-4 enable setting.
choices.feedback: The profile display proves configuration, not AP runtime behavior.

choices.text: That the AP received the profile and is transmitting on a permitted channel.
choices.feedback: Operational state must be verified on the AP and in the regulatory domain.

choices.text: That the selected FortiAP model belongs to the supported G-series family.
choices.feedback: A profile selection alone does not prove the deployed hardware model.

questions.question: After an upgrade, an HTTP bookmark to the Admin GUI stops working while the canonical HTTPS URL is reachable. What best explains the behavior?

choices.text: The RADIUS service has disabled all web sessions.
choices.feedback: RADIUS authentication does not explain browser HTTP-to-HTTPS enforcement.

choices.text: HSTS causes the browser to upgrade or refuse HTTP for the host.
choices.feedback: HSTS is cached by the browser after an HTTPS response and enforces HTTPS on later navigation.

choices.text: The Admin GUI has changed its management VLAN.
choices.feedback: A VLAN change would affect reachability, not specifically browser HSTS behavior.

choices.text: The FortiNAC database has purged the administrator account.
choices.feedback: The symptom is protocol handling, not evidence of account deletion.

questions.question: Which response is the strongest first verification for HSTS behavior?

choices.text: Rebuild the FortiNAC host inventory to refresh browser security headers.
choices.feedback: Host inventory does not verify the Admin GUI's HTTPS response.

choices.text: Clear browser HSTS state and disable certificate validation temporarily.
choices.feedback: That hides the symptom and weakens TLS validation without fixing the cause.

choices.text: Send a RADIUS Access-Request to confirm the Admin GUI's HTTPS behavior.
choices.feedback: RADIUS does not expose the web response header or certificate.

choices.text: Inspect the HTTPS response header and certificate chain for the canonical hostname.
choices.feedback: This verifies HSTS delivery and the TLS endpoint used by the browser.

questions.question: Why can a certificate hostname mismatch become more visible after HSTS is enabled?

choices.text: The browser stops validating the certificate after it caches HSTS.
choices.feedback: HSTS enforces HTTPS but does not bypass certificate validation.

choices.text: HSTS automatically adds the GUI hostname to the certificate SAN list.
choices.feedback: The certificate must already contain the correct subject alternative name.

choices.text: The browser will not fall back to insecure HTTP when HTTPS validation fails.
choices.feedback: HSTS makes certificate defects a hard HTTPS failure rather than a downgrade.

choices.text: The browser sends administrator credentials inside the HSTS response header.
choices.feedback: The header carries transport policy, not user credentials.

questions.question: Which statement about the documented FortiNAC version boundary is accurate?

choices.text: Admin GUI HSTS is enabled by default in 9.4.5+, 7.2.4+, and 7.4.0+.
choices.feedback: Those are the version families listed in the FortiNAC What's New documentation.

choices.text: HSTS is enabled only on FortiNAC-F 7.6.5.
choices.feedback: The cited version boundary is for FortiNAC Admin GUI, not that FortiNAC-F release.

choices.text: HSTS is enabled only after a RADIUS client sends Accounting-Start.
choices.feedback: HSTS is a web response header, unrelated to RADIUS accounting.

choices.text: HSTS is controlled by the switch's DHCP snooping configuration.
choices.feedback: DHCP snooping does not control the Admin GUI security header.

questions.question: The EAP-TLS log reaches CertificateVerify and then reports wrong curve for an ECDSA P-384 client certificate. What does that most strongly indicate?

choices.text: The VLAN assignment failed after Access-Accept.
choices.feedback: The failure occurs before a successful RADIUS authorization result.

choices.text: The switch never forwarded the EAP identity response.
choices.feedback: The handshake progressed far beyond the initial EAP identity exchange.

choices.text: The issuing CA is definitely missing from trust.
choices.feedback: The documented comparison showed the issuing CAs were already trusted.

choices.text: The server-side supported-curve set rejected the client's signature curve.
choices.feedback: The documented failure occurs at CertificateVerify after earlier certificate processing.

questions.question: The same client and port succeed with RSA-2048 but fail with ECDSA P-384. What is the best inference?

choices.text: The access switch is randomly dropping all EAP packets.
choices.feedback: RSA success on the same path argues against a general EAP transport failure.

choices.text: The key type isolates a curve-support boundary more than a switch-port fault.
choices.feedback: Holding client and port constant while changing certificate key type isolates the curve variable.

choices.text: The RADIUS shared secret is incorrect for ECDSA only.
choices.feedback: The shared secret is independent of the client certificate curve.

choices.text: The production VLAN has no DHCP scope.
choices.feedback: The failure occurs during TLS before VLAN assignment.

questions.question: Which remediation is supported by the documented P-384 scenario?

choices.text: Remove the issuing CA from Endpoint Trust and retry.
choices.feedback: The CA was already trusted; removing it would worsen certificate validation.

choices.text: Recreate every switch port and change its native VLAN.
choices.feedback: The issue is server-side curve support, not port configuration.

choices.text: Upgrade to FortiNAC-F 7.6.5 GA or later with backup and maintenance planning.
choices.feedback: The Community article states 7.6.5 GA+ supports ECDSA P-384 and recommends backup before upgrade.

choices.text: Disable all certificate validation for local RADIUS.
choices.feedback: That bypasses trust and does not address the supported-curve limitation safely.

questions.question: What does reaching CertificateVerify prove in this failure trace?

choices.text: The handshake passed earlier negotiation and certificate processing before signature-curve evaluation.
choices.feedback: The failure point is later than the initial certificate exchange.

choices.text: The client was already granted network access.
choices.feedback: Access-Accept follows successful EAP completion.

choices.text: The switch has installed the correct VLAN.
choices.feedback: VLAN authorization has not yet completed.

choices.text: The user password was validated by LDAP.
choices.feedback: EAP-TLS certificate authentication does not prove an LDAP password check.

questions.question: A RADSec client connects to FortiAuthenticator. Which certificate does the client need to present?

choices.text: The FortiAuthenticator server certificate copied into the client's user store.
choices.feedback: The server certificate authenticates FAC to the client; it is not the client's identity certificate.

choices.text: A client certificate issued by a CA configured as Local or Trusted on FortiAuthenticator.
choices.feedback: FAC validates the RADSec client's certificate issuer during the TLS handshake.

choices.text: A certificate signed by any public CA without FAC trust configuration.
choices.feedback: The client issuer must be in FAC's configured Local or Trusted CA stores.

choices.text: A certificate containing the RADIUS shared secret as a SAN.
choices.feedback: The shared secret is not encoded as a certificate SAN.

questions.question: Users receive Access-Accept over a separate authentication path, but no accounting sessions appear over RADSec. What should be tested separately?

choices.text: The FortiSwitch VNI-to-VLAN mapping.
choices.feedback: VXLAN mapping does not verify RADSec accounting ingestion.

choices.text: The user's browser HSTS cache.
choices.feedback: Browser transport policy does not verify RADIUS accounting.

choices.text: The FortiGate route-map-out-preferable field.
choices.feedback: BGP route advertisement policy does not carry accounting records.

choices.text: Accounting-Start, Interim-Update and Stop delivery over the RADSec connection.
choices.feedback: Authentication success does not prove the accounting client is sending the accounting message types.

questions.question: What is the default RADSec listener port documented for FortiAuthenticator?

choices.feedback: The Administration Guide identifies 2083 as the default configurable RADSec port.
1812 is a common UDP RADIUS authentication port, not the documented RADSec default.
4789 is the standard VXLAN UDP destination port.
179 is the BGP TCP port.

questions.question: Which statement about the documented RADSec scale boundary is correct?

choices.text: The guide limits all RADIUS users to 500 total accounts.
choices.feedback: The limit is simultaneous RADSec clients, not user database size.

choices.text: The guide guarantees 500 accounting messages per second.
choices.feedback: Concurrent client count is not a throughput guarantee.

choices.text: The guide documents up to 500 simultaneous RADSec clients.
choices.feedback: The Administration Guide gives a maximum of 500 concurrent RADSec clients.

choices.text: The guide requires exactly 500 client certificates.
choices.feedback: The number is a maximum concurrent connection count.

questions.question: A user is removed from a privileged SCIM group and no longer matches any Auto Provision Rule. What is the documented result?

choices.text: The user is converted automatically to a local administrator.
choices.feedback: No such fallback behavior is documented.

choices.text: The user keeps the last role until the next password rotation.
choices.feedback: SCIM updates trigger immediate authorization reevaluation.

choices.text: Only the display name is updated while secret access remains unchanged.
choices.feedback: The documented behavior includes deprovisioning and session enforcement.

choices.text: The user is de-authenticated and purged, and active login sessions are terminated.
choices.feedback: FortiPAM documents de-authentication/purge and termination when no APL matches.

questions.question: Why bind the SAML SSO server to a SCIM profile?

choices.text: It allows FortiPAM to decrypt the user's browser session.
choices.feedback: SCIM profile binding is identity lifecycle mapping, not TLS decryption.

choices.text: It links SAML-authenticated identities to SCIM-synchronized user and group data.
choices.feedback: SAML proves identity; the SCIM profile supplies lifecycle/group context for APL mapping.

choices.text: It replaces all secret policies with group membership alone.
choices.feedback: Secret policies remain a separate authorization layer.

choices.text: It disables Auto Provision Rules for remote users.
choices.feedback: The SCIM workflow uses APL rules to assign roles and permissions.

questions.question: A SCIM group change removes access to a secret while the user is in an active launch session. What should the operator expect?

choices.text: Only future SAML logins are affected; current launches are untouched.
choices.feedback: The documented behavior explicitly includes ongoing launch sessions.

choices.text: The session remains valid until the user logs out voluntarily.
choices.feedback: Immediate enforcement is part of the SCIM feature.

choices.text: FortiPAM reevaluates authorization and terminates launch sessions that are no longer authorized.
choices.feedback: The guide documents immediate reevaluation and termination of affected secret launches.

choices.text: The target password is automatically rotated on every group change.
choices.feedback: Password rotation is not the described SCIM enforcement action.

questions.question: A SAML login succeeds but the user receives the wrong secret permissions. Which evidence chain is most useful?

choices.text: SCIM group/attributes, selected SCIM profile, matched APL and resulting access profile.
choices.feedback: Those objects connect identity lifecycle data to the role FortiPAM assigned.

choices.text: The target server's default gateway and ARP table.
choices.feedback: Those do not explain FortiPAM's identity-to-role mapping.

choices.text: The FortiGate VPN tunnel MTU and TCP MSS.
choices.feedback: Tunnel MTU does not determine APL selection.

choices.text: The browser's HSTS max-age and certificate SAN.
choices.feedback: HSTS does not assign secret permissions.

questions.question: What factors does FortiSIEM document as inputs to Device and User Risk Scoring?

choices.text: Only IP reputation and interface utilization.
choices.feedback: Those are not the complete documented factor set.

choices.text: Asset criticality, user importance, incident severity/frequency and vulnerabilities.
choices.feedback: Those are the documented contextual factors combined into the score.

choices.text: Only the number of open TCP sessions and DNS queries.
choices.feedback: The documented score includes business and security context, not just traffic volume.

choices.text: Only the most recent incident's severity.
choices.feedback: The score also includes criticality, role/importance, frequency and vulnerabilities.

questions.question: A high-risk score appears for a user. What is the correct operational interpretation?

choices.text: Ignore the score because composite risk values cannot prioritize investigations.
choices.feedback: FortiSIEM provides the score and factor drill-down specifically for prioritization.

choices.text: Disable the account immediately without reviewing its incident evidence.
choices.feedback: Containment should be based on the underlying incident evidence and response policy.

choices.text: Assume the identity mapping and asset context are correct without checking.
choices.feedback: Incorrect CMDB or identity mapping can distort the score.

choices.text: Use factor drill-down to prioritize investigation; the score alone is not compromise proof.
choices.feedback: A composite score guides triage but is not a deterministic verdict.

questions.question: A critical server has a surprisingly low score despite several severe incidents. What should be checked first?

choices.text: The FortiGate's preferred outbound route map.
choices.feedback: BGP advertisement policy does not determine the SIEM risk score.

choices.text: The switch's PoE class and LLDP neighbor table.
choices.feedback: Those do not explain FortiSIEM risk factor lineage.

choices.text: Entity association, asset criticality, incident mapping and vulnerability context.
choices.feedback: Missing or incorrect enrichment can understate the entity's business and threat context.

choices.text: The SAML browser selected for FortiSASE.
choices.feedback: That authentication flow is unrelated to FortiSIEM entity scoring.

questions.question: Why should an analyst inspect score factor lineage instead of comparing only the numeric value?

choices.text: Different entities can reach similar scores through different incident, criticality and vulnerability combinations.
choices.feedback: The drill-down exposes the underlying factors that explain why the score was assigned.

choices.text: The dashboard score is randomly generated on each refresh.
choices.feedback: The documentation describes contextual factors and drill-down, not random scoring.

choices.text: The score is a direct copy of the highest incident severity.
choices.feedback: The score combines multiple factors rather than only one incident.

choices.text: The score cannot change when asset context changes.
choices.feedback: Asset criticality and user importance are explicit scoring factors.

questions.question: The FortiSASE profile shows Allow FIDO authentication, but FIDO is not offered to the user. Which prerequisite is essential?

choices.text: Disable SAML authentication so FortiClient can offer FIDO directly.
choices.feedback: FIDO is part of the configured SAML identity flow.

choices.text: Use a static IPv4 address and DHCP relay before enabling passkeys.
choices.feedback: Address assignment is not the FIDO profile prerequisite.

choices.text: Set the custom tunnel to UDP port 4789 before enabling FIDO2.
choices.feedback: 4789 is the VXLAN port and is unrelated to the SAML browser prerequisite.

choices.text: Enable SSO authentication and FortiClient's embedded SAML browser.
choices.feedback: Both SSO and the embedded browser are prerequisites for the FIDO option.

questions.question: macOS uses passkeys successfully, but Windows still prompts for a password with the same FortiSASE profile. What additional Windows setting is documented?

choices.text: Enable UNII-4 channels on the endpoint's wireless adapter.
choices.feedback: Radio channels do not control SAML authentication methods.

choices.text: Configure FIDO2 in the Entra ID Enterprise Application used for FortiSASE SAML SSO.
choices.feedback: Windows requires the FIDO2 method in the Entra enterprise application as well as the FortiSASE profile setting.

choices.text: Increase the FortiSASE IPsec DPD retry count to 10.
choices.feedback: DPD does not enable FIDO authentication.

choices.text: Add the endpoint's MAC address to a FortiNAC isolation VLAN.
choices.feedback: Network access VLAN assignment does not configure Entra FIDO2.

questions.question: A FIDO2 sign-in succeeds but the IPsec tunnel does not establish. Which boundary should be investigated next?

choices.text: The FortiSIEM user risk score.
choices.feedback: Risk scoring does not establish the IPsec tunnel.

choices.text: The FIDO authenticator's passkey registration history only.
choices.feedback: The FIDO ceremony succeeded, so tunnel parameters are the next boundary.

choices.text: Tunnel gateway parameters, certificate/IKE settings and endpoint-profile consistency.
choices.feedback: Successful SAML authentication moves the failure boundary to tunnel negotiation.

choices.text: The FortiNAC HSTS header.
choices.feedback: The Admin GUI security header is unrelated to tunnel negotiation.

questions.question: What does the embedded FortiClient browser contribute to this FIDO flow?

choices.text: It supplies the SAML user-agent path where the Entra FIDO2 challenge occurs.
choices.feedback: The embedded browser carries the SAML identity flow and passkey challenge.

choices.text: It performs IPsec encryption and IKE key exchange inside the browser.
choices.feedback: Tunnel cryptography is handled by FortiClient, not the browser.

choices.text: It replaces Entra ID as the configured SAML identity provider.
choices.feedback: Entra remains the identity provider and performs the FIDO2 challenge.

choices.text: It selects the endpoint's SD-WAN member during tunnel startup.
choices.feedback: The browser does not choose the endpoint's WAN member.

questions.question: Why does BGP on loopback reduce hub scale compared with BGP per overlay?

choices.text: It removes the need for spokes to advertise LAN prefixes to their hubs.
choices.feedback: Spoke LAN routes are still advertised; the reduction is in session count.

choices.text: Each spoke keeps one iBGP session per hub instead of one per overlay tunnel.
choices.feedback: Loopback peering reduces the number of overlay-specific BGP sessions.

choices.text: It moves every BGP session onto the physical WAN interface addresses.
choices.feedback: BGP on loopback uses stable loopback identities, not physical WAN addresses.

choices.text: It replaces ADVPN shortcut discovery with manually configured static routes.
choices.feedback: ADVPN shortcut discovery remains a separate mechanism.

questions.question: What does Dynamic BGP add to an ADVPN shortcut?

choices.text: It replaces the need for all SD-WAN underlay health checks.
choices.feedback: ADVPN 2.0 still uses underlay link-health criteria.

choices.text: It creates a second IPsec tunnel from each spoke to every hub.
choices.feedback: Dynamic BGP forms a spoke-to-spoke session over the shortcut.

choices.text: It installs a static default route on every FortiGate interface.
choices.feedback: A default route may be needed for reachability but is not Dynamic BGP.

choices.text: It forms a direct spoke-to-spoke BGP session over the shortcut for route exchange.
choices.feedback: This is the route-exchange behavior added by Dynamic BGP.

questions.question: User traffic moves to a new shortcut after an SLA failure, but the dynamic BGP session remains on the old shortcut. What explains this?

choices.text: Shortcut/data-plane movement and BGP session migration have different lifecycles; idle expiry may flush the old shortcut.
choices.feedback: The Community scenario documents traffic moving before the dynamic BGP session migrates.

choices.text: The new shortcut cannot carry IP traffic until BGP is restarted.
choices.feedback: The observed traffic movement disproves that conclusion.

choices.text: BGP always follows the exact same SLA state instantly as user traffic.
choices.feedback: The documented behavior shows a timing difference between the two state machines.

choices.text: The hub must re-advertise every spoke prefix before any shortcut can pass traffic.
choices.feedback: Dynamic BGP is intended to remove that route-reflector dependency.

questions.question: Why should the SLA server not be the remote BGP peer loopback in the documented ADVPN design?

choices.text: The SLA engine requires a multicast target for each spoke peer.
choices.feedback: The issue is route persistence to the health-check destination, not multicast.

choices.text: The peer loopback cannot be advertised through the overlay BGP process.
choices.feedback: The loopback is intended to provide a stable BGP identity.

choices.text: A persistent kernel route to the health-check target can pin BGP traffic after SLA failure.
choices.feedback: The Community scenario warns that the route can keep the control session on the same tunnel.

choices.text: The BGP peer must use UDP 4789 for all SLA probes.
choices.feedback: BGP uses TCP; 4789 is the VXLAN UDP port.

questions.question: A spoke cannot trigger a shortcut for a destination in another VRF. Which route check is most relevant?

choices.text: Verify hub loopback reachability and BGP next-hop resolution in the PE VRF.
choices.feedback: This is plausible but does not prove the spoke has a route in the VRF that must trigger the shortcut.

choices.text: Verify the ADVPN shortcut idle timer and BGP neighbor keepalive values.
choices.feedback: Those timers affect session lifecycle after a shortcut exists, not initial reachability.

choices.text: Verify the local route map and BGP community policy for the remote prefix.
choices.feedback: Route-map policy affects route advertisement after reachability is established.

choices.text: Verify hub/default-route reachability in the VRF that must trigger shortcut creation.
choices.feedback: The required hub reachability must exist in the VRF where shortcut initiation occurs.

questions.question: Which set of evidence best proves that the dynamic BGP control plane moved to the new shortcut?

choices.text: Only a successful ping between the two LAN hosts.
choices.feedback: Ping proves reachability but not which tunnel carries BGP or how routes were learned.

choices.text: BGP neighbor state/path, RIB recursive next hop, shortcut state and per-VRF SLA.
choices.feedback: These views distinguish the BGP session, installed route, shortcut and health state.

choices.text: Only the hub's global BGP neighbor count.
choices.feedback: A global count does not identify the spoke-to-spoke session path.

choices.text: Only the FortiManager overlay template wizard status.
choices.feedback: Template generation does not prove runtime session or route state.
